claim: Mind-wandering during reading involves retrieving autobiographical information that is unrelated to the text.
source: While reading, our mind can wander to unrelated autobiographical information, creating a perceptually decoupled state detrimental to narrative comprehension.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a premise of the study.

claim: Mind-wandering during reading creates a perceptually decoupled state.
source: While reading, our mind can wander to unrelated autobiographical information, creating a perceptually decoupled state detrimental to narrative comprehension.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a central hypothesis of the study.

claim: Perceptual decoupling during mind-wandering is detrimental to narrative comprehension.
source: While reading, our mind can wander to unrelated autobiographical information, creating a perceptually decoupled state detrimental to narrative comprehension.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by the experimental findings.

claim: Medial regions of the default mode network (DMN) were recruited during memory retrieval in Experiment 1.
source: Medial regions of the default mode network (DMN) were recruited during memory retrieval.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the fMRI data in Experiment 1.

claim: Left temporal and lateral prefrontal regions of the DMN were recruited when reading for comprehension in Experiment 1.
source: In contrast, left temporal and lateral prefrontal regions of the DMN, as well as ventral visual cortex, were recruited when reading for comprehension.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the fMRI data in Experiment 1.

claim: Ventral visual cortex was recruited when reading for comprehension in Experiment 1.
source: In contrast, left temporal and lateral prefrontal regions of the DMN, as well as ventral visual cortex, were recruited when reading for comprehension.
evidence: This is a direct finding from the fMRI data in Experiment 1.

claim: DMN regions linked to memory are more functionally decoupled from regions of ventral visual cortex than regions in the same network engaged when reading.
source: Experiment two used functional connectivity both at rest and during tasks to establish that (i) DMN regions linked to memory are more functionally decoupled from regions of ventral visual cortex than regions in the same network engaged when reading
evidence: This is a finding from the functional connectivity analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Individuals with more self-generated mental contents and poorer comprehension while reading in the lab showed more decoupling between visually connected DMN sites important for reading and primary visual cortex.
source: and (ii) individuals with more self-generated mental contents and poorer comprehension, while reading in the lab, showed more decoupling between visually connected DMN sites important for reading and primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the individual differences analysis in Experiment 2.

claim: Greater coupling between DMN sites and visual cortex was observed when participants reported greater focus on reading in the face of conflict from autobiographical memory cues.
source: A similar pattern of connectivity was found in Experiment 1, with greater coupling between this DMN site and visual cortex when participants reported greater focus on reading in the face of conflict from autobiographical memory cues
evidence: This is a finding from the task-based functional connectivity analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: The retrieval of personally relevant memories increased the decoupling of DMN sites from visual cortex.
source: moreover, the retrieval of personally relevant memories increased the decoupling of these sites.
evidence: This is a finding from the task-based functional connectivity analysis in Experiment 1.

claim: Generating autobiographical mental content relies on cortical regions within the DMN which are functionally decoupled from ventral visual regions engaged during reading.
source: These converging data suggest we lose track of the narrative when our minds wander because generating autobiographical mental content relies on cortical regions within the DMN which are functionally decoupled from ventral visual regions engaged during reading.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined findings of Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Self-generated states are common in daily life.
source: Although self-generated states are common in daily life (Kane et al., 2007; Poerio et al., 2013), they can be problematic if they occur during reading (McVay and Kane, 2012; Smallwood et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Self-generated states can be problematic if they occur during reading.
source: Although self-generated states are common in daily life (Kane et al., 2007; Poerio et al., 2013), they can be problematic if they occur during reading (McVay and Kane, 2012; Smallwood et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The detrimental effects of mind-wandering on reading occur because this state elicits perceptual decoupling that disrupts narrative comprehension.
source: The detrimental effects of mind-wandering on reading are believed to occur because this state elicits perceptual decoupling that disrupts narrative comprehension (Smallwood, 2011; Smallwood, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Reading for comprehension is linked to activity within the default mode network (DMN).
source: Contemporary work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that both reading for comprehension (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014b; Binder et al., 2009; Mar, 2011; Yang et al., 2019), and off-task states (Christoff et al., 2009; Konu et al., 2020), are linked to activity within the default mode network (DMN).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Off-task states are linked to activity within the default mode network (DMN).
source: Contemporary work in cognitive neuroscience has shown that both reading for comprehension (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014b; Binder et al., 2009; Mar, 2011; Yang et al., 2019), and off-task states (Christoff et al., 2009; Konu et al., 2020), are linked to activity within the default mode network (DMN).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The building blocks of reading for comprehension are conceptual representations supported by regions overlapping with DMN in the anterior, ventral and lateral temporal lobe.
source: For example, the building blocks of reading for comprehension are conceptual representations supported by regions overlapping with DMN in the anterior, ventral and lateral temporal lobe (Lambon Ralph et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The content of self-generated thoughts often comes from autobiographical memory.
source: In contrast, the content of self-generated thoughts often comes from autobiographical memory (Smallwood et al., 2011), linked to medial regions of the DMN including posterior cingulate, ventral prefrontal and inferior parietal cortex (Ritchey and Cooper, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Autobiographical memory is linked to medial regions of the DMN including posterior cingulate, ventral prefrontal and inferior parietal cortex.
source: In contrast, the content of self-generated thoughts often comes from autobiographical memory (Smallwood et al., 2011), linked to medial regions of the DMN including posterior cingulate, ventral prefrontal and inferior parietal cortex (Ritchey and Cooper, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Individuals who are better at reading for comprehension show more functional integration between lateral and medial elements of the DMN.
source: For example, individuals who are better at reading for comprehension show more functional integration between lateral and medial elements of the DMN, while individuals who tend to be more off-task show greater decoupling between the DMN and regions of visual cortex important for visual processing during reading (Smallwood et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Individuals who tend to be more off-task show greater decoupling between the DMN and regions of visual cortex important for visual processing during reading.
source: For example, individuals who are better at reading for comprehension show more functional integration between lateral and medial elements of the DMN, while individuals who tend to be more off-task show greater decoupling between the DMN and regions of visual cortex important for visual processing during reading (Smallwood et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN's role in cognition emerges from this system's topographic location, with core nodes located in regions that are distant in both functional and structural terms from unimodal cortex.
source: Recent views suggest the DMN's role in cognition emerges from this system's topographic location, with core nodes located in regions that are distant in both functional and structural terms from unimodal cortex (Margulies et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The topographical organisation of the DMN explains its role in multiple cognitive states because it locates this network at the end of information processing streams necessary for relatively abstract tasks like reading comprehension.
source: This topographical organisation has been argued to explain the role of the DMN in multiple cognitive states because it locates this network at the end of information processing streams that are necessary for relatively abstract tasks (like reading comprehension) but also explains why the same network can be involved in states that require disengagement from the here and now (such as mind-wandering; Smallwood et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The topographical organisation of the DMN explains why the same network can be involved in states that require disengagement from the here and now such as mind-wandering.
source: This topographical organisation has been argued to explain the role of the DMN in multiple cognitive states because it locates this network at the end of information processing streams that are necessary for relatively abstract tasks (like reading comprehension) but also explains why the same network can be involved in states that require disengagement from the here and now (such as mind-wandering; Smallwood et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The process of generating mental content using information from memory leads to a perceptually decoupled state associated with poor comprehension.
source: This topographically informed view of the DMN provides a novel hypothesis for why mind-wandering creates a situation in which we lose track of the meaning of the words we are reading: the process of generating mental content using information from memory leads to a perceptually decoupled state associated with poor comprehension.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: When mind-wandering occurs during reading, there is a shift in the balance of neural activity within the DMN, away from DMN regions functionally coupled with ventral visual regions important for reading comprehension, to other regions within DMN that are more isolated from perceptual input.
source: When this occurs, there is a shift in the balance of neural activity within the DMN, away from DMN regions functionally coupled with ventral visual regions important for reading comprehension, to other regions within DMN that are more isolated from perceptual input.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: In Experiment 1, participants performed tasks that mimicked the experience of mind-wandering while reading.
source: In Experiment 1, participants (N = 29) performed tasks that mimicked the experience of mind-wandering while reading.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: In Experiment 2, the functional architecture of regions involved in reading and autobiographical memory was examined to evaluate whether the DMN regions important for reading are more functionally connected to the ventral visual stream than the DMN regions involved in autobiographical memory.
source: Experiment 2 examined the functional architecture of regions involved in these two states, evaluating whether the DMN regions important for reading are more functionally connected to the ventral visual stream than the DMN regions involved in autobiographical memory (N = 243).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Left lateral prefrontal and temporal regions of the DMN, within the dorsomedial subsystem, are important for reading.
source: Foreshadowing our results, we found that (a) left lateral prefrontal and temporal regions of the DMN, within the dorsomedial subsystem (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011), are important for reading, while regions of the core DMN are engaged during autobiographical memory (medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate, and angular gyrus)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Regions of the core DMN are engaged during autobiographical memory, including medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate, and angular gyrus.
source: Foreshadowing our results, we found that (a) left lateral prefrontal and temporal regions of the DMN, within the dorsomedial subsystem (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2010; Yeo et al., 2011), are important for reading, while regions of the core DMN are engaged during autobiographical memory (medial prefrontal, posterior cingulate, and angular gyrus)
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Regions of the DMN linked to reading are more functionally connected to ventral visual regions than DMN regions implicated in autobiographical memory.
source: (b) regions of the DMN linked to reading are more functionally connected to ventral visual regions than DMN regions implicated in autobiographical memory
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: DMN regions linked to reading are decoupled from primary visual cortex for individuals who naturally generate more mind-wandering content during reading.
source: (c) DMN regions linked to reading are decoupled from primary visual cortex for individuals who naturally generate more mind-wandering content during reading, generalising our experimental paradigm to an ecologically valid situation
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The perceptual decoupling pattern linked to individual variation in mind-wandering during reading is modulated by task manipulation, with greater perceptual decoupling during the retrieval of personally relevant memories in the absence of sentences.
source: and (d) this perceptual decoupling pattern linked to individual variation in mind-wandering during reading is also modulated by our task manipulation, with greater perceptual decoupling during the retrieval of personally relevant memories in the absence of sentences and less decoupling when participants remain focussed on reading despite distracting autobiographical memory cues.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the task-based connectivity analysis.

claim: There is less perceptual decoupling when participants remain focussed on reading despite distracting autobiographical memory cues.
source: and (d) this perceptual decoupling pattern linked to individual variation in mind-wandering during reading is also modulated by our task manipulation, with greater perceptual decoupling during the retrieval of personally relevant memories in the absence of sentences and less decoupling when participants remain focussed on reading despite distracting autobiographical memory cues.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the task-based connectivity analysis.

claim: The reason we lose track of the narrative when our mind wanders during reading is because the generation of autobiographical content relies on neural activity in core DMN regions and this encourages a state of perceptual decoupling that reduces comprehension of external input.
source: Our analysis, therefore, suggests that the reason we lose track of the narrative when our mind wanders during reading is because the generation of autobiographical content relies on neural activity in core DMN regions and this encourages a state of perceptual decoupling that reduces comprehension of external input.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined findings.

claim: Participants reported reduced task focus on the primary task for both reading and autobiographical memory retrieval when both tasks were presented at the same time.
source: Participants reported reduced task focus on the primary task for both reading and autobiographical memory retrieval when both tasks were presented at the same time (i.e., in Conflict conditions), F(1,28) = 44.28, p < 0.001, ηp2 = .61 (see panel A in the right hand of Figure 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no interaction between Task and Conflict on task focus ratings.
source: There was no interaction between Task and Conflict, F(1,28) = .12, p = 0.73, ηp2 = .004, indicating that the effect of conflict between tasks had an equivalent effect on mental focus in reading and autobiographical memory.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The effect of conflict between tasks had an equivalent effect on mental focus in reading and autobiographical memory.
source: There was no interaction between Task and Conflict, F(1,28) = .12, p = 0.73, ηp2 = .004, indicating that the effect of conflict between tasks had an equivalent effect on mental focus in reading and autobiographical memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical finding.

claim: Retrieval of autobiographical memories reduced rated comprehension during reading trials.
source: For the reading trials, retrieval of autobiographical memories reduced rated comprehension, F(1,28) = 10.40, p = 0.003, ηp2 = .27, but not participants' level of prior familiarity with the sentence material, F(1,28) = 2.10, p = 0.16, ηp2 = .07 (see panel B in the right hand of Figure 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Retrieval of autobiographical memories did not affect participants' level of prior familiarity with the sentence material.
source: For the reading trials, retrieval of autobiographical memories reduced rated comprehension, F(1,28) = 10.40, p = 0.003, ηp2 = .27, but not participants' level of prior familiarity with the sentence material, F(1,28) = 2.10, p = 0.16, ηp2 = .07 (see panel B in the right hand of Figure 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Concurrent presentation of meaningful text reduced the vividness of the memories that were retrieved during autobiographical memory trials.
source: For autobiographical memory, concurrent presentation of meaningful text reduced the vividness of the memories that were retrieved, F(1,28) = 36.29, p < 0.001, ηp2 = .56, as well as the rated consistency between retrieval in the scanner and the memory described for the cue word outside the scanner, F(1,28) = 8.19, p = 0.008, ηp2 = .23 (see panel C in the right hand of Figure 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Concurrent presentation of meaningful text reduced the rated consistency between retrieval in the scanner and the memory described for the cue word outside the scanner.
source: For autobiographical memory, concurrent presentation of meaningful text reduced the vividness of the memories that were retrieved, F(1,28) = 36.29, p < 0.001, ηp2 = .56, as well as the rated consistency between retrieval in the scanner and the memory described for the cue word outside the scanner, F(1,28) = 8.19, p = 0.008, ηp2 = .23 (see panel C in the right hand of Figure 1).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The paradigm successfully captures important features of the mind-wandering reading state, particularly the mutual inhibition between self-generated mental content and effective reading for comprehension.
source: This pattern establishes that our paradigm successfully captures important features of the mind-wandering reading state, particularly the mutual inhibition between self-generated mental content and effective reading for comprehension.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral findings.

claim: Reading was associated with greater neural activity in a set of left lateralised regions within the temporal lobe and prefrontal cortex, including inferior frontal gyrus and superior and middle temporal gyri.
source: Contrasting reading with autobiographical memory retrieval highlighted a set of left lateralised regions within the temporal lobe and prefrontal cortex, including inferior frontal gyrus and superior and middle temporal gyri, which are recruited during reading.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Activation in bilateral ventral visual cortex was observed during reading.
source: Activation in bilateral ventral visual cortex was also observed.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Periods when autobiographical memory was the primary task were associated with greater neural activity in regions including medial and lateral prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and angular gyrus.
source: In contrast, periods when autobiographical memory was the primary task were associated with greater neural activity in regions including medial and lateral prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex and angular gyrus.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Regions showing greater activity during reading are associated with functional terms such as 'reading' and 'language' according to Neurosynth meta-analysis.
source: As expected, there was a correspondence between the psychological features of our conditions and the functional terms revealed by the meta-analysis, with regions linked to reading associated with terms such as 'reading' and 'language', while regions linked to autobiographical memory retrieval associated with terms like 'memory retrieval' and 'episodic'.
evidence: This is based on meta-analytic decoding using Neurosynth, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Regions showing greater activity during autobiographical memory retrieval are associated with functional terms like 'memory retrieval' and 'episodic' according to Neurosynth meta-analysis.
source: As expected, there was a correspondence between the psychological features of our conditions and the functional terms revealed by the meta-analysis, with regions linked to reading associated with terms such as 'reading' and 'language', while regions linked to autobiographical memory retrieval associated with terms like 'memory retrieval' and 'episodic'.
evidence: This is based on meta-analytic decoding using Neurosynth, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The DMN regions engaged during reading were entirely within the dorsomedial system (100%).
source: It can be seen that the DMN regions engaged during reading were entirely within the dorsomedial system (red; 100%), while the majority of the DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the core subsystem (blue; 78%), with equal percentages in the dorsomedial (red; 11%) and medial temporal subsystems (green; 11%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The majority of the DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the core subsystem (78%).
source: It can be seen that the DMN regions engaged during reading were entirely within the dorsomedial system (red; 100%), while the majority of the DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the core subsystem (blue; 78%), with equal percentages in the dorsomedial (red; 11%) and medial temporal subsystems (green; 11%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 11% of DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the dorsomedial subsystem.
source: It can be seen that the DMN regions engaged during reading were entirely within the dorsomedial system (red; 100%), while the majority of the DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the core subsystem (blue; 78%), with equal percentages in the dorsomedial (red; 11%) and medial temporal subsystems (green; 11%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 11% of DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the medial temporal subsystem.
source: It can be seen that the DMN regions engaged during reading were entirely within the dorsomedial system (red; 100%), while the majority of the DMN voxels showing higher activity during autobiographical memory retrieval fell within the core subsystem (blue; 78%), with equal percentages in the dorsomedial (red; 11%) and medial temporal subsystems (green; 11%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Regions in medial prefrontal and parietal cortex, superior frontal gyrus and left lateral parietal cortex showed a stronger effect of task focus for autobiographical memory retrieval, relative to reading.
source: The results of this analysis are presented in Figure 3A where it can be seen that regions in medial prefrontal and parietal cortex, superior frontal gyrus and left lateral parietal cortex showed a stronger effect of task focus for autobiographical memory retrieval, relative to reading.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Clusters linked to better task focus for autobiographical memory retrieval also showed stronger activity during memory retrieval and lower activity during reading.
source: Figure 3B shows that clusters linked to better task focus for autobiographical memory retrieval also showed stronger activity during memory retrieval and lower activity during reading.
evidence: This is based on a formal conjunction analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Greater task focus during memory retrieval was associated with increased activation in medial prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex (bordering dorsal lateral occipital cortex), superior frontal gyrus, retrosplenial cortex, and temporal fusiform cortex.
source: Greater task focus during memory retrieval was associated with increased activation in medial prefrontal cortex, posterior parietal cortex (bordering dorsal lateral occipital cortex), superior frontal gyrus, retrosplenial cortex, and temporal fusiform cortex.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Voxels showing greater task focus during memory retrieval largely fell within the medial temporal subsystem (50% of voxels within DMN) and core subsystem (40% of DMN voxels).
source: These voxels largely fell within the medial temporal subsystem (50% of voxels within DMN) and core subsystem (40% of DMN voxels); there was less overlap with the dorsomedial DMN subsystem (10%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems.

claim: Greater task focus in reading was correlated with increased deactivation in overlapping regions in bilateral middle and medial frontal gyrus, frontal pole, insular cortex, anterior/posterior cingulate gyrus, precuneus and angular gyrus.
source: In contrast, greater task focus in reading was correlated with increased deactivation in overlapping regions in bilateral middle and medial frontal gyrus, frontal pole, insular cortex, anterior/posterior cingulate gyrus, precuneus and angular gyrus.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1.

claim: Voxels showing greater task focus in reading largely fell within core DMN (82% of DMN voxels), with limited overlap in dorsomedial and medial temporal DMN subsystems (13% and 5% of DMN voxels, respectively).
source: These voxels largely fell within core DMN (82% of DMN voxels), with limited overlap in dorsomedial and medial temporal DMN subsystems (13% and 5% of DMN voxels, respectively).
evidence: This is based on analysis of DMN subsystems.

claim: When people are more focussed on autobiographical memories, there is increased activation in core and medial temporal DMN regions.
source: Therefore, when people are more focussed on autobiographical memories, there is increased activation in core and medial temporal DMN regions, while deactivation of core DMN regions is linked to greater mental focus during reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuroimaging findings.

claim: Deactivation of core DMN regions is linked to greater mental focus during reading.
source: Therefore, when people are more focussed on autobiographical memories, there is increased activation in core and medial temporal DMN regions, while deactivation of core DMN regions is linked to greater mental focus during reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuroimaging findings.

claim: Regions of ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and superior frontal gyrus contribute to better focus on autobiographical memory retrieval while compromising the ability to read for comprehension.
source: Taken together, this analysis establishes that regions of ventromedial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex, and superior frontal gyrus contribute to better focus on autobiographical memory retrieval while compromising the ability to read for comprehension.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neuroimaging findings.

claim: The reading DMN region showed greater intrinsic connectivity to regions of ventral visual cortex.
source: The reading DMN region showed greater intrinsic connectivity to regions of ventral visual cortex.
evidence: This is a resting-state connectivity finding from Experiment 2.

claim: There was stronger intrinsic connectivity for the reading than the autobiographical memory DMN seed to a visual site implicated during reading.
source: A paired samples t-test revealed stronger intrinsic connectivity for the reading than the autobiographical memory DMN seed to this visual site implicated during reading (Reading DMN-to-Reading visual: Mean ± SD = 0.02 ± 0.14, Autobiographical memory DMN-to-Reading visual: Mean ± SD = –0.01 ± 0.14; t(242) = 2.78, p = 0.006).
evidence: This is a resting-state connectivity finding from Experiment 2, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: The DMN and visual regions showing stronger activation during reading than memory retrieval also had stronger intrinsic connectivity at rest.
source: This analysis provides further evidence that the DMN and visual regions showing stronger activation during reading than memory retrieval also had stronger intrinsic connectivity at rest.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resting-state connectivity findings.

claim: The functional connectivity of regions linked to reading is mirrored by their joint activation during reading.
source: This 'task-rest' conjunction establishes that the functional connectivity of regions linked to reading is mirrored by their joint activation during reading, suggesting that co-activation of aspects of DMN and visual cortex during reading is at least partially rooted in their intrinsic functional organisation.
evidence: This is based on a formal conjunction analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Co-activation of aspects of DMN and visual cortex during reading is at least partially rooted in their intrinsic functional organisation.
source: This 'task-rest' conjunction establishes that the functional connectivity of regions linked to reading is mirrored by their joint activation during reading, suggesting that co-activation of aspects of DMN and visual cortex during reading is at least partially rooted in their intrinsic functional organisation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the conjunction analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Group-level regression using the DMN site showing peak activation during reading as a seed demonstrated stronger connectivity with regions in primary visual cortex and postcentral gyrus in individuals with good comprehension and less reported mind-wandering content.
source: Group-level regression, using the DMN site showing peak activation during reading as a seed, demonstrated stronger connectivity with regions in primary visual cortex and postcentral gyrus in individuals with good comprehension and less reported mind-wandering content.
evidence: This is a resting-state connectivity finding from Experiment 2, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Weaker intrinsic connectivity between visually coupled DMN regions and the visual cortex is associated with a tendency to mind-wander while reading.
source: In summary, weaker intrinsic connectivity between visually coupled DMN regions and the visual cortex is associated with a tendency to mind-wander while reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the individual differences findings from Experiment 2.

claim: This analysis establishes a link between the experimental manipulation that mimics key processes engaged during mind-wandering in reading, and a metric describing a naturally occurring example of the state.
source: Importantly, this analysis establishes a link between our experimental manipulation that mimics key processes engaged during mind-wandering in reading, and a metric describing a naturally occurring example of the state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings linking Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: There was a significant interaction between Task and Conflict for the Reading DMN seed connectivity to visual cortex.
source: However, there was a significant interaction between Task and Conflict, F(1,27) = 5.42, p = 0.028, ηp2 = .17.
evidence: This is a task-based connectivity finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant effect of Task in the absence of conflict, reflecting higher connectivity between the reading DMN seed and visual cortex when participants were reading.
source: Post-hoc t-tests revealed a significant effect of Task in the absence of conflict, t(27) = 2.81, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.018 for two tests, reflecting higher connectivity between the reading DMN seed and visual cortex when participants were reading.
evidence: This is a task-based connectivity finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: There was no effect of Task in the conflict condition for Reading DMN seed connectivity to visual cortex.
source: There was no effect of Task in the conflict condition, t(27) = 0.21, Bonferroni-corrected p = 1 for two tests, consistent with the view that conflict from autobiographical memory can disrupt visual connectivity to DMN during reading.
evidence: This is a task-based connectivity finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Conflict from autobiographical memory can disrupt visual connectivity to DMN during reading.
source: There was no effect of Task in the conflict condition, t(27) = 0.21, Bonferroni-corrected p = 1 for two tests, consistent with the view that conflict from autobiographical memory can disrupt visual connectivity to DMN during reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task-based connectivity finding.

claim: For the parametric effects of Task Focus, there was a significant interaction effect between Task and Conflict for Reading DMN seed connectivity to visual cortex.
source: There was a significant interaction effect between these two factors, F(1,27) = 6.54, p = 0.016, ηp2 = .20.
evidence: This is a task-based connectivity finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: When participants were more focussed on reading in the face of distraction from autobiographical memory cues, connectivity between the reading DMN seed and visual cortex was higher.
source: Post-hoc t-tests found a significant main effect of Task in the conflict condition, t(27) = 2.62, Bonferroni-corrected p = 0.030 for two tests, when participants were more focussed on reading in the face of distraction from autobiographical memory cues, connectivity between the reading DMN seed and visual cortex was higher.
evidence: This is a task-based connectivity finding from Experiment 1, supported by statistical analysis.

claim: Reading-related DMN decouples from visual cortex when participants retrieve personally relevant memories in the absence of sentences.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that reading-related DMN decouples from visual cortex when participants retrieve personally relevant memories in the absence of sentences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task-based connectivity findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: When reading and memory retrieval are in conflict, reading-related DMN sites couple with visual cortex when participants are more focussed on reading and decouple when participants are more focussed on autobiographical memories.
source: When reading and memory retrieval are in conflict, these sites couple when participants are more focussed on reading and decouple when participants are more focussed on autobiographical memories.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the task-based connectivity findings shown in Figure 5.

claim: This analysis establishes a similar perceptual decoupling pattern for this visual site in both naturally occurring and experimentally mimicked experiences of mind-wandering during reading.
source: Importantly, this analysis establishes a similar perceptual decoupling pattern for this visual site in both naturally occurring and experimentally mimicked experiences of mind-wandering during reading, highlighting the importance of perceptual decoupling when memory retrieval competes with reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the task-based and resting-state findings.

claim: Perceptual decoupling is important when memory retrieval competes with reading.
source: Importantly, this analysis establishes a similar perceptual decoupling pattern for this visual site in both naturally occurring and experimentally mimicked experiences of mind-wandering during reading, highlighting the importance of perceptual decoupling when memory retrieval competes with reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Experiment 1 established a pattern of mutual inhibition between the act of reading for comprehension and the concurrent retrieval of autobiographically-relevant content.
source: Experiment 1 established a pattern of mutual inhibition between the act of reading for comprehension and the concurrent retrieval of autobiographically-relevant content.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: The pattern of mutual inhibition between reading and autobiographical memory retrieval parallels the well-established negative correlation between naturally occurring mind-wandering and an individual's ability to comprehend what they are reading.
source: This pattern of mutual inhibition parallels the well-established negative correlation between naturally occurring mind-wandering and an individual's ability to comprehend what they are reading (McVay and Kane, 2012; Smallwood et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the experimental findings to prior research.

claim: Reading for comprehension and autobiographical memory retrieval differentially recruited different aspects of the DMN in direct contrasts of these two tasks.
source: Using fMRI to index brain activity, we identified that these two states differentially recruited different aspects of the DMN in direct contrasts of these two tasks, with greater recruitment of the dorsomedial DMN subnetwork when participants were reading for comprehension, and greater activity within the core of the DMN during autobiographical memory retrieval (See also Chiou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from Experiment 1.

claim: There was greater recruitment of the dorsomedial DMN subnetwork when participants were reading for comprehension.
source: Using fMRI to index brain activity, we identified that these two states differentially recruited different aspects of the DMN in direct contrasts of these two tasks, with greater recruitment of the dorsomedial DMN subnetwork when participants were reading for comprehension, and greater activity within the core of the DMN during autobiographical memory retrieval (See also Chiou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from Experiment 1.

claim: There was greater activity within the core of the DMN during autobiographical memory retrieval.
source: Using fMRI to index brain activity, we identified that these two states differentially recruited different aspects of the DMN in direct contrasts of these two tasks, with greater recruitment of the dorsomedial DMN subnetwork when participants were reading for comprehension, and greater activity within the core of the DMN during autobiographical memory retrieval (See also Chiou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from Experiment 1.

claim: The involvement of the DMN in both self-generated mental content and reading for comprehension is consistent with prior studies exploring trait variation in mind-wandering while reading.
source: The involvement of the DMN in both self-generated mental content and reading for comprehension is consistent with prior studies exploring trait variation in mind-wandering while reading (Smallwood et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking the findings to prior research.

claim: Ventral visual regions were engaged when participants were reading for comprehension as opposed to engaged in autobiographical memory recall.
source: Importantly, Experiment one found that ventral visual regions were engaged when participants were reading for comprehension as opposed to engaged in autobiographical memory recall, a pattern consistent with the view that the retrieval of autobiographical memories during mind-wandering creates a perceptually decoupled state (Schooler et al., 2011; Smallwood, 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of neuroimaging findings from Experiment 1.

claim: The retrieval of autobiographical memories during mind-wandering creates a perceptually decoupled state.
source: Importantly, Experiment one found that ventral visual regions were engaged when participants were reading for comprehension as opposed to engaged in autobiographical memory recall, a pattern consistent with the view that the retrieval of autobiographical memories during mind-wandering creates a perceptually decoupled state (Schooler et al., 2011; Smallwood, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: There is strong intrinsic coupling between regions of DMN relevant to reading and ventral visual cortex.
source: Experiment 2 used resting-state functional connectivity to establish that there is strong intrinsic coupling between regions of DMN relevant to reading and ventral visual cortex
evidence: This is a summary of resting-state connectivity findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Regions of core DMN, activated by autobiographical memory retrieval, showed reduced correlation with ventral visual regions, compared with aspects of DMN linked to reading.
source: in contrast, regions of core DMN, activated by autobiographical memory retrieval, showed reduced correlation with these ventral visual regions, compared with aspects of DMN linked to reading.
evidence: This is a summary of resting-state connectivity findings from Experiment 2.

claim: The reduction of activity in ventral visual cortex observed in Experiment 1 was not an artefact of task instructions which required participants to attend to autobiographical memories rather than textual input.
source: This pattern suggests that the reduction of activity in ventral visual cortex observed in Experiment 1 was not an artefact of our task instructions which required participants to attend to autobiographical memories rather than textual input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resting-state connectivity findings.

claim: The core DMN regions activated when we retrieve autobiographical memories are functionally distant from regions of ventral visual cortex important for reading comprehension.
source: Instead, the core DMN regions activated when we retrieve autobiographical memories are functionally distant from regions of ventral visual cortex important for reading comprehension.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resting-state connectivity findings.

claim: In individuals who remained focussed on reading and who had better comprehension, primary visual cortex showed stronger functional coupling to the aspects of DMN that support reading.
source: We found that, in individuals who remained focussed on reading and who had better comprehension, primary visual cortex showed stronger functional coupling to the aspects of DMN that support reading.
evidence: This is a summary of individual differences findings from Experiment 2.

claim: For people who generated more off-task thought contents, regions of visual cortex showed weaker functional coupling to reading-relevant DMN regions.
source: For people who generated more off-task thought contents, these regions of visual cortex showed weaker functional coupling to reading-relevant DMN regions.
evidence: This is a summary of individual differences findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Decoupling of a reading-related DMN site to visual cortex was greater during the retrieval of autobiographical memories in the absence of sentences.
source: This perceptual decoupling pattern was also seen in our task-based functional connectivity analysis of Experiment 1, since we found that decoupling of a reading-related DMN site to visual cortex was greater during the retrieval of autobiographical memories in the absence of sentences and when there was better focus on memory retrieval in the face of distracting semantic inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of task-based connectivity findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Decoupling of a reading-related DMN site to visual cortex was greater when there was better focus on memory retrieval in the face of distracting semantic inputs.
source: This perceptual decoupling pattern was also seen in our task-based functional connectivity analysis of Experiment 1, since we found that decoupling of a reading-related DMN site to visual cortex was greater during the retrieval of autobiographical memories in the absence of sentences and when there was better focus on memory retrieval in the face of distracting semantic inputs.
evidence: This is a summary of task-based connectivity findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Simply asking individuals to retrieve autobiographical information creates a perceptually decoupled state that is at odds with the comprehension of information from the external environment.
source: Psychologically, our study suggests that simply asking individuals to retrieve autobiographical information creates a perceptually decoupled state that is at odds with the comprehension of information from the external environment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Perceptual decoupling is related to the persistence of self-generated mental content in consciousness.
source: This pattern is consistent with the view that perceptual decoupling is related to the persistence of self-generated mental content in consciousness (Smallwood, 2013).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: Mind-wandering while reading involves a shift in the balance of neural activity within the DMN, away from lateral temporal and prefrontal regions that are closely linked to regions of ventral visual cortex important for reading, and towards regions within the core of this system involved in supporting mental content that is unrelated to the external environment during autobiographical memory retrieval.
source: In the neural domain, our data suggests that mind-wandering while reading involves a shift in the balance of neural activity within the DMN, away from lateral temporal and prefrontal regions that are closely linked to regions of ventral visual cortex important for reading, and towards regions within the core of this system involved in supporting mental content that is unrelated to the external environment during autobiographical memory retrieval.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings.

claim: Studies that have established the role of the DMN in explicit memory retrieval also show that this pattern is accompanied by the suppression of visual processing.
source: In this context, it is worth noting that studies that have established the role of the DMN in explicit memory retrieval also show that this pattern is accompanied by the suppression of visual processing (Murphy et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Individuals with epilepsy who are impaired in the process of pattern separation necessary for accurate episodic memory retrieval show atypical suppression of brain activity in visual cortex during memory retrieval.
source: Furthermore, individuals with epilepsy who are impaired in the process of pattern separation necessary for accurate episodic memory retrieval show atypical suppression of brain activity in visual cortex during memory retrieval (Li et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Antagonistic activity patterns in the DMN and in sensory cortices may be important for features of memory retrieval to proceed in an effective manner.
source: The current data, therefore, provide novel support for the possibility that antagonistic activity patterns in the DMN and in sensory cortices may be important for features of memory retrieval to proceed in an effective manner.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior research.

claim: The broader DMN can support apparently antagonistic states, particularly both perceptually coupled and decoupled modes of cognition.
source: More generally, our data add to growing evidence for a broad contribution of the DMN to features of human cognition. In particular, our findings are consistent with observations that the broader DMN can support apparently antagonistic states, particularly both perceptually coupled and decoupled modes of cognition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of broader DMN function.

claim: The DMN plays a key role in the integration of internal and external information in the service of aligning the perspectives of different individuals over time.
source: Recently, however, Yeshurun et al., 2021 have argued that the DMN plays a key role in the integration of internal and external information in the service of aligning the perspectives of different individuals over time.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work.

claim: The role of the broader DMN in reading for comprehension is consistent with the perspective that this mode of operation could help to create common ground between different individuals in their understanding of a narrative.
source: Our data highlighting the role of the broader DMN in reading for comprehension is consistent with this perspective, as this mode of operation could help to create common ground between different individuals in their understanding of a narrative.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of prior theoretical work.

claim: The involvement of the DMN in situations such as mind-wandering can lead to a breakdown in the common ground between individuals by impairing comprehension during reading.
source: However, the involvement of the same broad system in situations such as mind-wandering suggests that it can also lead to a breakdown in the common ground between individuals, in this case by impairing comprehension during reading.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Both operational modes of the DMN stem from topographic location of DMN at the end of sensory processing streams, such as the ventral visual stream.
source: Both of these operational modes stem from topographic location of DMN at the end of sensory processing streams, such as the ventral visual stream.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of DMN topography.

claim: The topographic location of the DMN allows this network to provide abstract representations of external information.
source: This allows this network to provide abstract representations of external information and, at the same time, the DMN's functional and structural distance to unimodal sensory systems provides the opportunity for decoupled states to emerge, which support mental contents that are unrelated to external input (such as self-generated off-task states; Margulies et al., 2016; Smallwood et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of DMN topography, supported by citations.

claim: The DMN's functional and structural distance to unimodal sensory systems provides the opportunity for decoupled states to emerge, which support mental contents that are unrelated to external input.
source: This allows this network to provide abstract representations of external information and, at the same time, the DMN's functional and structural distance to unimodal sensory systems provides the opportunity for decoupled states to emerge, which support mental contents that are unrelated to external input (such as self-generated off-task states; Margulies et al., 2016; Smallwood et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the context of DMN topography, supported by citations.

claim: Lateral temporal and frontal regions within dorsomedial DMN activate in response to both reading and autobiographical memory retrieval tasks.
source: Although different aspects of the DMN play distinctive roles in reading comprehension and autobiographical memory retrieval, there are still some neural similarities between these two mental states; since the lateral temporal and frontal regions within dorsomedial DMN activate in response to both tasks (i.e., identified by a formal conjunction across the contrast maps of each task over the letter string baseline; see Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1, shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Previous studies have shown the engagement of lateral temporal and inferior frontal cortex in both reading and memory recall.
source: Previous studies have shown the engagement of lateral temporal and inferior frontal cortex in both reading and memory recall (Andrews-Hanna et al., 2014a; Ferstl et al., 2008; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Summerfield et al., 2009; Svoboda et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Both reading and memory recall tasks involve semantic cognition.
source: Given that both tasks involve semantic cognition (e.g. Dehaene et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2003; Spitsyna et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006), this finding is consistent with prior work implicating lateral temporal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus in the representation and retrieval of heteromodal conceptual knowledge (Badre et al., 2005; Binder et al., 2009; Jefferies, 2013; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Lateral temporal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus are implicated in the representation and retrieval of heteromodal conceptual knowledge.
source: Given that both tasks involve semantic cognition (e.g. Dehaene et al., 2015; Graham et al., 2003; Spitsyna et al., 2006; Svoboda et al., 2006), this finding is consistent with prior work implicating lateral temporal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus in the representation and retrieval of heteromodal conceptual knowledge (Badre et al., 2005; Binder et al., 2009; Jefferies, 2013; Lambon Ralph et al., 2017; Noonan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The regions important for reading comprehension activate not only when visual input is task-relevant (i.e., during reading for comprehension), but also when this input is irrelevant to the ongoing task (i.e., revealed by autobiographical memory retrieval with conflict > autobiographical memory retrieval with no conflict).
source: In addition, we found that the regions important for reading comprehension activate not only when visual input is task-relevant (i.e., during reading for comprehension), but also when this input is irrelevant to the ongoing task (i.e., revealed by autobiographical memory retrieval with conflict > autobiographical memory retrieval with no conflict; see Appendix 1—figure 5), and irrespective of task focus.
evidence: This is a neuroimaging finding from Experiment 1, shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: Reading-relevant regions may be more perceptually coupled supporting visual to conceptual knowledge mapping.
source: In line with our findings, these reading-relevant regions may be more perceptually coupled supporting visual to conceptual knowledge mapping.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Reading-relevant regions might be sensitive to situations in which meaning emerges in the external environment, even when the focus of attention is elsewhere.
source: In this way, they might be sensitive to situations in which meaning emerges in the external environment, even when the focus of attention is elsewhere.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings.

claim: In both Experiment 1, and in many examples of naturally occurring mind-wandering, the off-task mental contents may have greater relevance to the individual than information in the environment.
source: First, in both Experiment 1, and in many examples of naturally occurring mind-wandering, the off-task mental contents may have greater relevance to the individual than information in the environment (Sanders et al., 2017; Smallwood et al., 2011), perhaps because these states rely on ventral regions of medial prefrontal cortex (Konu et al., 2020) that are important for motivated states (Kouneiher et al., 2009; Rushworth et al., 2004; Stawarczyk and D'Argembeau, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Off-task mental states may rely on ventral regions of medial prefrontal cortex that are important for motivated states.
source: First, in both Experiment 1, and in many examples of naturally occurring mind-wandering, the off-task mental contents may have greater relevance to the individual than information in the environment (Sanders et al., 2017; Smallwood et al., 2011), perhaps because these states rely on ventral regions of medial prefrontal cortex (Konu et al., 2020) that are important for motivated states (Kouneiher et al., 2009; Rushworth et al., 2004; Stawarczyk and D'Argembeau, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Different types of self-generated thoughts have different neural correlates.
source: Third, contemporary studies suggest that different types of self-generated thoughts have different neural correlates (Karapanagiotidis et al., 2020; Mckeown et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Certain features of naturally occurring off-task thought patterns could lead to greater or lesser disengagement from external input.
source: Accordingly, it is possible that certain features of naturally occurring off-task thought patterns could lead to greater or lesser disengagement from external input.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: For Experiment 1, 29 undergraduate students were recruited (age-range 18–23, mean age ± SD = 20.14 ± 1.26, 6 males).
source: For Experiment 1, 29 undergraduate students were recruited (age-range 18–23, mean age ± SD = 20.14 ± 1.26, 6 males).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: For Experiment 2, one sample consisted of 244 participants (age-range 18–31, mean age ± SD = 20.73 ± 2.39, 77 males; three participants overlapped with Experiment 1).
source: For Experiment 2, we used two separate resting-state samples: one sample consisted of 244 participants (age-range 18–31, mean age ± SD = 20.73 ± 2.39, 77 males; three participants overlapped with Experiment 1), which was used to examine the intrinsic connectivity of DMN regions linked to reading and autobiographical memory retrieval.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: One participant was excluded from Experiment 2 analysis due to excessive head motion (i.e., mean head motion > 0.4 mm).
source: One participant was excluded from this analysis due to excessive head motion (i.e., mean head motion > 0.4 mm).
evidence: This describes data exclusion criteria.

claim: Another published dataset of 69 participants (age range 18–31, mean age ± SD = 19.87 ± 2.33, 26 males; without any participant overlap with the other two samples) was used to characterise the relationship of functional architecture of the DMN regions associated with reading and autobiographical memory retrieval and individual variation in naturally occurring mind-wandering reading.
source: Another published dataset of 69 participants (age range 18–31, mean age ± SD = 19.87 ± 2.33, 26 males; without any participant overlap with the other two samples) was used to characterise the relationship of functional architecture of the DMN regions associated with reading and autobiographical memory retrieval and individual variation in naturally occurring mind-wandering reading, as measured in our prior study (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the participant sample.
